source_neutral.procedure: Examine one approval route for one case type, represented as an ordered list of checkpoints from submission at checkpoint 0 to final approval at checkpoint n. Each adjacent pair defines one handoff. For a fixed cohort, classify each examined checkpoint according to whether cumulative elapsed time from submission exceeds the cumulative allowance for reaching it. Fix the classification rule before examining data; an example is whether the cohort median exceeds the allowance. The two classifications are within allowance and behind allowance. Starting with a verified early checkpoint within allowance and a verified late checkpoint behind allowance, repeatedly examine a checkpoint near the middle of the unresolved interval and reduce that interval according to its classification. The process ends with one handoff, a wider interval containing unobservable checkpoints, or a halt without a result under the specified conditions.
source_neutral.action: Fix the case type, cohort, ordered checkpoint list, allowances and classification rule. Verify that the submission timestamp represents the actual start of the request rather than later ticket creation, and that the cohort's end-to-end elapsed time exceeds the total allowance under the same rule. Select the checkpoint nearest the middle of the unresolved interval. Obtain the cohort's cumulative elapsed time to that checkpoint from ticket histories, reconstruct its time, or add temporary logging for that checkpoint alone. Apply the fixed classification rule. If the checkpoint is behind allowance, discard the later portion of the interval and use it as the new late endpoint. If it is within allowance, discard the earlier portion and use it as the new early endpoint. If its time cannot be recovered, skip it, examine an adjacent checkpoint and record that the final interval may consequently be wider. Repeat on the remaining interval, using the same cohort for every examination where possible.
source_neutral.observables: Each checkpoint examination yields a binary classification, within allowance or behind allowance, with the underlying elapsed-time figures retained. Across examinations, record the shrinking interval between the latest checkpoint classified within allowance and the earliest checkpoint classified behind allowance. With n handoffs and all checkpoints observable, roughly log2(n) examinations are needed. Also record skipped checkpoints, classifications close to the allowance, and disagreement between the first and second comparable cohorts at the final interval endpoints. During the pilot, record whether classification changes at the checkpoint immediately after the localized handoff and at final approval.
source_neutral.inferential_warrant: For the examined case type and cohort, the reported result places the first transition from cumulative elapsed time within allowance to cumulative elapsed time behind allowance in the final unresolved handoff, or in the final interval when checkpoints have been skipped. That handoff is the priority candidate for inspection of exceptional cases, interviews and a bounded pilot. The result alone does not establish that the handoff is the sole or largest source of delay or that it causes the delay. If a change confined to the handoff is followed by within-allowance classifications immediately after it and at final approval under comparable demand and staffing, this supports, without proving, that the handoff contributed materially and that the change is a workable bounded remedy for this case type. If the checkpoint after the handoff improves while final approval remains behind allowance, the procedure interprets this as further delay accumulating elsewhere and repeats the search. These conclusions remain subject to the limitations on interval reduction, measurement and comparison.
source_neutral.problem_decomposition: The units are one case type, one approval route, a cohort of cases, ordered checkpoints, adjacent-checkpoint handoffs, checkpoint timestamps, cumulative elapsed times, cumulative allowances and a fixed classification rule. The unresolved interval is bounded by an early checkpoint within allowance and a late checkpoint behind allowance. Each examination divides this interval, and the classification determines which portion is retained. Parallel approvals and rework loops must be collapsed into single checkpoints to make the route's order unambiguous. The identified handoff is connected to upstream submissions, approvers who may serve other routes, downstream batching and other handoffs that may contribute delay. Follow-up compares classification immediately after the localized handoff with classification at final approval, allowing improvement at the handoff to be distinguished from the end-to-end outcome.
source_neutral.next_inquiry: After localization, reclassify the two checkpoints bounding the localized handoff using a second comparable cohort. Use the handoff as the priority candidate for inspection of exceptional cases and interviews. Pilot one change confined to that handoff. Illustrative candidates are assigning a named owner, stating a response window or changing the review batching schedule; these are not established remedies. Reapply the same classification at the checkpoint immediately after the handoff and at final approval under comparable demand and staffing. If final approval remains behind allowance after the pilot, re-establish the endpoints and repeat the interval reduction on the remaining route.
source_neutral.limits: Before starting, the early endpoint must be verified within allowance, including confirmation that the recorded submission time is the real request start. The late endpoint must be verified behind allowance using the same classification rule. The route must be sequential for the selected case type, with parallel approvals and rework loops collapsed into checkpoints, and the cohort must come from a period of comparable demand and staffing. The supplied information does not establish that checkpoint-level allowances exist or can be agreed in advance: service-level targets are mentioned without specifying their granularity. It also does not establish that checkpoint times can be recovered from ticket histories or captured through temporary logging. Stop with a localized result when the unresolved interval is one handoff between adjacent checkpoints. Stop with a partial result when all remaining checkpoints are unobservable, reporting the interval of several handoffs. Halt without a result if an endpoint fails verification or a checkpoint changes classification when checked on a second comparable cohort. High case-to-case variability or a small cohort can cause classifications to change between cohorts; classifications close to the allowance are unreliable. Checkpoints without recoverable times, informal handoffs and parallel approvals cannot be examined and leave a multi-handoff interval. A cohort may be behind allowance at one checkpoint and recover downstream, and rework loops may return cases to earlier stages; discarding half the route after one examination can therefore exclude a real contributor. When delay is distributed across several handoffs, the localized transition identifies where the cumulative total crosses the allowance, and that location changes if allowances are set differently. Waiting at the identified handoff may originate in incomplete upstream submissions, an approver shared with other routes or downstream batching. The transition is correlated with delay without establishing the handoff as its sole cause. A start timestamp later than the actual request, a final timestamp recording ticket closure instead of the approval decision, or a cohort that is not actually late directs the search to the wrong interval. Status-change timestamps do not separate waiting time from working time within a stage. Prospective logging takes calendar time, during which demand and staffing may change between examinations. Mixing case types with different routes invalidates the ordering. The procedure locates a position on the route and does not determine when the delay began. Results apply to the examined case type and period. Pilot comparisons remain observational unless demand and staffing are comparable. If ticket histories already timestamp every handoff, all checkpoints can be classified at once, and examining them in halving order saves no effort over comparing timestamps stage by stage. The cost justification for halving applies where each checkpoint time must be reconstructed or newly logged.
